Question: are there any *conceptual* differences between "free trade" in-country versus trade across borders?

International trade is a whole different ballgame, because the international system is essentially anarchy. There are a few international organizations, such as the WTO, which set up trade rules, but they rely on members to enforce those.

Internationally, what we describe as "free trade" is when one or more nations have either entered a free trade agreement, or joined an organization such as the WTO. There are rules about tariffs, rules about currency manipulation, human rights rules, etc. Disputes are usually settled by another party, or a body that is established by the agreement.

So conceptually free trade internationally is totally different. We're talking about an organized system where you opt in or form your own agreements, and then participate according to the rules agreed to by all parties (fun fact, China is basically violating all the rules).

Intrastate free trade you're operating by default on the same rules as everyone else, since they're governmental rules (or lack thereof). You don't need any kind of special treaty or agreements to engage in trade within your own country.

TL;DR: International free trade is when countries agree on rules to reduce trade barriers; intrastate free trade is when the government allows citizens to trade with each other freely and with minimal restriction.
